# Handguns and muskets (matchlock, flintlock) (`handguns_muskets`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs gunpowder; helped by cannon_artillery, bloomery_iron, wire_drawing
- Core idea: A wrought-iron tube forged round a mandrel and welded along the seam, closed by a screwed breech plug, mounted on a wooden stock shaped to the shoulder. In the matchlock a pivoted arm lowers a smouldering cord, soaked in saltpetre, into a small pan of fine priming powder beside the touch hole when the trigger is squeezed, so the firer can keep both hands on the gun and his eye on the target. The flintlock replaces the match with a flint striking a hinged steel plate, which also uncovers the pan. A smoothbore musket hits a man reliably at 50 to 80 m and fires two or three rounds a minute, so it works only in massed, drilled volleys.
- Pitfalls:
  - A lit match near loose powder; matchlock men blew themselves and their neighbours up regularly
  - Describing a flintlock as easy; its springs and hardened steel face need a skilled locksmith
  - Expecting accuracy from a smoothbore; early guns won because a recruit learns them in weeks and the ball pierces armour, not because they outshot the bow
  - Rain and wind put out match and priming
  - A badly welded barrel splits at the seam
- History: china: 1132 – fire lances at the siege of De'an (a 10th c. painting from Dunhuang may show one); c. 1288 – metal hand cannon; 1548–1558 – matchlocks copied from Portuguese and Japanese models; europe: 14th c. – hand cannon on a pole; c. 1411 – first picture of a serpentine match holder; c. 1470s – matchlock arquebus with sprung lock and shoulder stock, the state of the art in 1490; c. 1500 – wheel lock; c. 1610 – true flintlock (Marin le Bourgeoys); by 1700 flintlock replaces matchlock; in 1683 most infantry still carry matchlocks; islamic: mid 15th c. – Janissaries carry arquebuses; 16th c. – Ottoman gunsmiths spread the matchlock from Morocco to Sumatra; east_asia: 1543 – Portuguese matchlocks reach Tanegashima, Japan; mass production within a decade; india: 1526 – Babur's matchlock men at Panipat
- Read:
  - Bert S. Hall, Weapons and Warfare in Renaissance Europe (1997)
  - Kenneth Chase, Firearms: A Global History to 1700 (2003)
